kernelIdea: re^{iθ} is the point at distance r from the origin at counterclockwise angle θ. Polar form is non-unique: re^{iθ} = re^{i(θ+2πk)}. Special values include e^{iπ} + 1 = 0.

kernels.l1: There are two ways to say where something is: across and up, or how far and which way.
kernels.l2: You can name a spot by how far across and up it is, or by how far away it is and which direction to face. Both names point at the same spot.
kernels.l3: A complex number can be described by distance and direction instead of across and up. Turning all the way around brings you back, so the direction has many names for the same point.
kernels.l4: A point can be named by its distance from the origin and the direction you face to reach it. Multiplying multiplies the distances and adds the turns, and the direction is only pinned down to within whole turns.
kernels.l5: A complex number can be described by how far out it is and how far round it has turned, instead of by across-and-up. Converting between the two descriptions needs the angle facts of the geometry course, and the turn is only ever pinned down to within a whole number of full turns.
kernels.l6: A point is named by its distance and its angle. The angle is only pinned down to within whole turns, and that is what forces a convention.
kernels.l7: Writing a point as r times a unit-circle point at angle θ makes multiplication easy; the angle is fixed only to within whole turns, so naming one official angle always costs a jump somewhere.
kernels.l8: A point is named by how far out and how far round, and the second is only fixed once you choose a range. That freedom is why the complex logarithm is genuinely many-valued.

kernel: re^{iθ} is the point at distance r from the origin at counterclockwise angle θ. Polar form is non-unique: re^{iθ} = re^{i(θ+2πk)}. Special values: i = e^{iπ/2}, −1 = e^{iπ}, and e^{iπ} + 1 = 0.
objectives: Convert between a + bi and re^{iθ}
